tips.rainy: Rain is active in your area — hold off on spraying pesticides, as it will wash off before working.
tips.rainyShort: Hold off on spraying — rain is active
tips.rainyLong: Rain is currently active in your area, and this changes what your crops need right now. Spraying pesticides or fertilizer during rain is largely wasted, since the water washes the product off leaves before it has time to work. This is also a good window to check your field drainage — standing water around root zones for more than a day can lead to root rot, especially in crops that aren't naturally water-tolerant. If your soil already tends to hold water, consider clearing any blocked drainage channels now while it's easy to see where water is pooling. Once the rain clears, give the field a day to firm up before walking heavy equipment across it, since wet soil compacts easily and that compaction can hurt root growth for weeks afterward. Hold off on any pesticide or fertilizer application until at least a few hours after the rain fully stops.
tips.hot: Temperatures are high today — irrigate early morning or evening to reduce water loss from evaporation.
tips.hotShort: Irrigate early morning or evening today
tips.hotLong: Today's high temperatures mean water evaporates much faster from the soil surface, so the timing of irrigation matters more than usual. Watering during the hottest part of the day wastes a significant portion of that water to evaporation before it ever reaches the roots. Early morning irrigation lets plants take up water before the day's heat stress begins, while evening irrigation gives the soil overnight to absorb moisture without competing against strong sun. Avoid watering the leaves themselves during peak heat, since water droplets can sometimes intensify sun damage on leaf surfaces. If your crop is at a sensitive growth stage — flowering or fruit-setting — extra attention to consistent moisture today can meaningfully protect yield. Keep an eye on wilting in the early afternoon; if leaves droop even after a normal morning watering, a light supplemental watering in the evening can help the plant recover overnight.
tips.cloudy: Cloudy skies today are a good time to check crops for early signs of pest activity without sun stress.
tips.cloudyShort: Good day to check for pests
tips.cloudyLong: Cloudy conditions today create comfortable conditions for both you and your crops, making it a genuinely good day to walk your fields carefully. Without harsh direct sun, you can spend more time closely inspecting leaves, stems, and the undersides of foliage, where many early pest infestations first appear. This is also a lower-stress day for the plants themselves, so any hands-on work like light pruning, tying up vines, or thinning is easier on the crop than it would be under strong sun. Overcast days are also often when humidity rises, which can accelerate fungal issues, so this is a good moment to check for early signs of mildew or leaf spot, particularly in densely planted areas with poor airflow. Cloud cover doesn't fully block UV, so don't skip basic sun protection for yourself while working, but overall this is one of the more comfortable and productive days to catch small problems before they spread.
tips.clear: Clear skies today are ideal for fieldwork like weeding, harvesting, or applying fertilizer.
tips.clearLong: Clear skies and dry conditions today make this an ideal window for the kind of fieldwork that's disrupted by rain or high humidity. Weeding is especially effective right now, since dry soil makes it easier to fully remove root systems rather than just breaking off the visible growth. If you're planning to harvest, dry conditions reduce the risk of mold or spoilage during storage, since moisture on harvested produce is one of the biggest causes of post-harvest loss. This is also a reliable day to apply granular fertilizer, since there's no risk of it washing away before the soil has a chance to absorb it — though you'll still want to water it in afterward rather than leaving it dry on the surface. If you've been waiting for a good day to repair fencing, clear irrigation channels, or move equipment across the field, today's stable weather removes most of the usual obstacles to that kind of maintenance work.
tips.cold: Cooler temperatures today - a good time to check for frost risk on sensitive young crops.
tips.coldLong: Cooler temperatures today raise the risk of frost, particularly overnight and in the early morning hours when temperatures typically drop further. Young seedlings and tender crops are especially vulnerable, since frost damage to new growth can set back development significantly or kill the plant outright in severe cases. If you have young or sensitive crops exposed, consider covering them overnight with cloth, straw mulch, or simple plastic sheeting to trap ground heat. Established, hardier crops usually tolerate mild cold better, but it's still worth checking for any wilting or discoloration the following morning as an early warning sign. Watering the soil lightly before a cold night can actually help, since moist soil holds heat better than dry soil and releases it slowly overnight. If frost does occur, avoid disturbing frost-damaged leaves early in the morning while they're still frozen, since handling them at that stage often causes more cell damage than the frost itself.
tips.windy: Windy conditions today - avoid spraying pesticides or fertilizer, as wind can cause uneven coverage.
tips.windyLong: Windy conditions today make spraying pesticides, fertilizer, or any liquid treatment significantly less effective and more wasteful than usual. Wind causes uneven coverage — some areas get too much product while others get almost none — and a meaningful portion can drift away from your field entirely, which is both a waste of money and a potential risk to neighboring crops or water sources. If treatment genuinely can't wait, consider spraying during any calmer window later in the day rather than in current conditions. Strong wind can also physically stress young or tall plants, so this is a good day to check for any leaning or breakage, especially in crops that haven't fully established their root systems yet. Loose mulch or lightweight coverings can blow away in strong wind, so it's worth checking that anything covering young seedlings is still secured. Save spraying tasks for tomorrow or a calmer part of today, and instead focus on wind-safe tasks like inspection, harvesting sturdier crops, or securing loose materials around the field.
tips.default: Check your crops today for early signs of pest activity, especially after any recent rain.
tips.defaultShort: Check crops for early pest signs
tips.defaultLong: With no extreme weather conditions to plan around today, this is a good opportunity to do a general, unhurried inspection of your crops rather than reacting to any specific weather risk. Walk your field methodically, checking the undersides of leaves and the base of stems, where early pest activity and disease symptoms are often easiest to spot before they spread further. If there's been any recent rain in the past few days, pay particular attention to signs of fungal growth or root stress, since lingering soil moisture can create conditions for problems that aren't immediately obvious from the surface. This is also a reasonable day to catch up on routine maintenance you may have been postponing — checking irrigation lines for leaks or blockages, tightening supports for climbing crops, or simply taking stock of which sections of the field are progressing well versus lagging behind. Keeping a simple record of what you observe today, even mentally, makes it much easier to notice meaningful changes on your next inspection.
